planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens or rooted cuttings in spring on a trellis, arbor, or fence in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; where winters dip below the upper 20s F, grow in a container that can be sheltered or expect hard dieback with root-level regrowth in spring.

directions: This glossy-leaved twining vine from the Admiralty Islands produces pinwheel-shaped white flowers, pink-blushed in bud, that open in flushes through the warm months and carry a light sweet fragrance most noticeable in the evening. It climbs by twining rather than tendrils, so give it wire, lattice, or an arbor to grasp, or shear it periodically to hold it as a mounding shrub or hedge instead of a climber. Established plants tolerate Gulf Coast heat and humidity well and recover quickly from pruning after a hard freeze. Feed lightly during the growing season and keep soil evenly moist but not waterlogged for the heaviest bloom.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost danger has passed; this white-flowered sport of king's mantle shares the species' unusual tolerance for blooming well in partially shaded sites.

directions: This selected form of king's mantle swaps the species' deep violet-purple trumpets for pure white flowers with a pale-yellow throat, set off by the same glossy, dark-green foliage that makes the species such a dependable partial-shade bloomer. It grows as a mounding, arching evergreen shrub with woody lower stems, flowering on new growth nearly continuously from spring through fall in warm weather. In zone 9 it typically freezes back in winter but resprouts reliably from the roots once soil warms in spring. Use it to brighten a shaded courtyard bed or pair it with the purple-flowered species for contrast along a partially shaded border.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring on a trellis, arbor, or fence in well-drained soil; grow it where it gets some relief from the hottest midday sun, since direct afternoon exposure can scorch the bright foliage in Gulf Coast summers.

directions: Grown chiefly for its vivid chartreuse-to-gold young foliage that matures to lime green, this common jasmine sport holds its bright color best with a few hours of morning sun and afternoon shade, making it a striking foliage accent as well as a bloomer. Like the species, it produces clusters of small, intensely fragrant white flowers in summer, though the foliage color is the main draw for most gardeners. Train the twining stems on a trellis or let them scramble through a shrub border, and prune after flowering to control size and encourage fresh colorful growth. Protect the roots with mulch where winters are borderline, since foliage color and vigor are best in climates milder than the species' hardiest range.
